metadata.title: Don't Invent the Mass.
metadata.purpose: A viewer with no physics or coding background can say what the parse step may and may not do, name its rules (engine vocabulary, SI units, no constants, keep letters as letters), and explain why a reading mistake is the one error later checks can't catch.

beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer — the ask lands answered
beats.narration_text: Hey, this is Param Madan, and this explainer video is on the parse step: the one place the physics engine lets an A.I. model touch the problem. Here's a mistake it used to make. A problem said: a particle of mass m. No number anywhere. And the parser wrote down, mass equals one.

props.command: A problem says "a particle of mass m" with no numbers. Why did the parser write m = 1.0, and how was it fixed?
output: Parse only reads; it never solves
It used to invent values for letters
Now a letter stays a letter, and SymPy solves it

beats.narration_text: In the next few minutes, you'll see three things. First, what the parse step is allowed to do, and what it isn't. Second, the rules that keep its reading honest. And third, the bug where it made up numbers, and how the team fixed it. No physics or coding background needed.

The answer up front. Parse has one job: reading comprehension. Pull out the stated quantities, and name what's being asked. It must not solve anything, rearrange a formula, or pick a value. Every step after this follows fixed rules. So a reading mistake here is the one mistake the rest of the engine can't catch. A wrong number goes in, and a carefully checked wrong answer comes out.

Rule one: use the engine's words. The formula cards call mass m, and starting speed v zero. Models like to invent their own names, like initial velocity, or mass one written out. So the engine translates every name into its own vocabulary. Before that fix, it once returned correct algebra written in the parser's words. Useless to a student, and impossible to match against an answer key.

beats.new_visual_element: SI units, no constants, rest means zero
beats.narration_text: Rule two: convert to standard units before reporting. Twenty-five kilometers becomes twenty-five thousand meters. One hundred microfarads becomes zero point zero zero zero one farads. One exception: angles stay in degrees. Rule three: don't report constants, like gravity. The engine adds those itself. And starts from rest is written down as a starting speed of zero.

Now the bug. Most problems in UGPhysics, the benchmark the team tested against, are written in symbols, not numbers. A particle of mass m, with charge q. The parser used to fill in numbers anyway. Mass, one point zero. Charge, one point zero. For a problem with no numbers in it at all. That produces an answer that looks checked, and is wrong.

The fix: if a quantity is given as a symbol, report it as a symbol. Don't invent a number. SymPy can do algebra with letters. Two masses, m one and m two, over a pulley. Acceleration equals g, times m two minus m one, over m one plus m two. And the check gets stronger. It simplifies to zero, which proves the answer holds for every value, not just one.

beats.new_visual_element: traceable, and not yet fully measured
beats.narration_text: Two more safeguards. Every value carries the exact phrase it came from, so a misread number can be traced back to its words. And a reply that can't be read at all is reported as a parse error, kept separate from a problem the engine simply doesn't cover. What's not proven yet: the team says parse quality hasn't been measured against a real model beyond spot checks. And because newer Claude models don't take a randomness setting, this one step can vary between runs.

So here's the takeaway for any A.I. answer. Check what it read before you check what it got. If a number shows up that wasn't in the problem, that's a guess. And everything built on it is wrong, however carefully it was checked.
Your turn. Paste this into Claude with any physics problem. It asks Claude to list only what the problem actually states, and to quote where each value came from.

props.command: Here is a physics problem: [paste it]. Before solving anything, list every known with its value in SI units, and quote the exact phrase it came from. If a quantity is given only as a letter, keep it as a letter — do not invent a number. Then list what is being asked.
output: Every known quoted from the problem

beats.new_visual_element: title restate, terracotta period, name beneath
beats.narration_text: Read first. Then solve. This has been Param Madan. Thanks for watching.
